title: The roadmap that cannot fit
prompt: You inherit a roadmap with twelve major features promised for the next quarter. The team has six engineers, two product managers, and no clear definition of what success means. What do you do before assigning work?
failure_modes: turning the roadmap into a ticket list

title: The deadline before discovery
prompt: A VP asks for a delivery date for a system nobody has built and whose dependencies are still uncertain. They want a number by tomorrow. How do you answer?

title: The impressive AI design
prompt: An AI assistant proposes a well-documented event-driven architecture with queues, state machines, retries, and a workflow engine for a product that currently processes fifty requests per day. What do you inspect before approving it?
failure_modes: rejecting it only because it is complex

title: Feature pressure versus foundation
prompt: Sales promises a large customer a feature that depends on a brittle subsystem. The feature could close the deal, but the subsystem is already causing incidents. How do you reason about the next two weeks?

title: The metric everyone can game
prompt: Leadership wants engineers measured by pull requests merged per week. You know the metric will distort behavior. What do you propose instead, and what will still go wrong?
failure_modes: offering a better proxy as truth

title: The bug that only appears after three days
prompt: A customer reports a data discrepancy that appears only after a long-running workflow completes. Logs are incomplete and the obvious reproduction path fails. How do you investigate?

title: The outage where the hero is wrong
prompt: Production is down. Your strongest engineer wants to bypass safeguards and hot-fix directly in production. They are usually right and the team trusts them. What do you do?
failure_modes: block action without a path forward
turning the outage into a power struggle

title: The subsystem only one person understands
prompt: A critical subsystem is effectively owned by one senior engineer. They are productive, protective, and overloaded. What do you change without destroying their autonomy?
failure_modes: treat the engineer as the problem

title: The code review nobody wants to write
prompt: A senior engineer's changes are consistently hard to review, but nobody comments because they are politically dangerous. How do you surface the issue?

title: Build versus buy is the wrong question
prompt: A team is arguing whether to build an internal tool or buy a vendor product. The argument has become ideological. What questions make the actual decision visible?

title: The migration while traffic keeps flowing
prompt: You need to replace a core datastore while the product remains live. There is no downtime window and no clean rollback. How do you decompose the migration?

title: The skill you keep avoiding
prompt: You know distributed systems would make you stronger, but you keep avoiding it because the material feels abstract and punishing. How do you build a learning plan that changes how you think rather than checking a box?

title: The junior engineer asks for the answer
prompt: A junior engineer asks you to solve a bug for them because they are behind. You can fix it in five minutes; they may spend two hours. What do you do?

title: The requirement that is really a wish
prompt: A stakeholder says, 'Make onboarding feel effortless.' No one can define effortless. What do you do before building?

title: The performance work nobody needs yet
prompt: An engineer wants to spend a sprint optimizing a path that is currently 8% of latency and not customer-visible. They are excited about the work. What do you do?
failure_modes: kill the idea because it is not urgent

title: The demo that skips the hard part
prompt: A product demo works beautifully because it stores sensitive data in a way security will reject. The team wants to launch it and 'fix security later.' How do you respond?

title: Everything is urgent
prompt: Three stakeholders all say their request is urgent. Each has a plausible business reason. How do you decide what is actually urgent?
failure_modes: build a scoring matrix and obey it blindly

title: The developer tool nobody adopts
prompt: You built an internal tool that should save engineers time, but they keep working around it. What do you investigate?

title: The green test suite that lies
prompt: CI is green, but customers keep seeing regressions. The team wants more tests. What do you ask before adding them?

title: The AI code review that sounds right
prompt: An AI review flags a risky design choice with polished reasoning, but the author says the review misunderstands the local constraint. How do you evaluate it?
failure_modes: trust AI because it sounds coherent

title: The team of brilliant specialists
prompt: You have five highly capable specialists. Delivery is slow because every change crosses two or three ownership boundaries. What do you change?

title: The prototype that became production
prompt: A prototype built for a demo now has paying customers. It is ugly but working. How do you decide whether to rewrite, harden, or leave it alone?
failure_modes: add abstractions without understanding failure modes

title: The promotion plan that is just more tasks
prompt: You want to become a staff engineer. Your manager says to 'take on more scope.' What actual capabilities do you need to develop?

title: The vendor lock-in argument
prompt: Someone says, 'We cannot use this cloud service because vendor lock-in is bad.' Another says, 'We should use it because it is fastest.' How do you reason about it?

title: Learning a language by building
prompt: You want to learn Rust, but every tutorial feels disconnected from real work. What project would force the important concepts without becoming a six-month detour?

title: The customer requests an API
prompt: A large customer asks for an API. The team wants to expose the current internal model. What do you examine before saying yes?

title: The on-call rotation that drains everyone
prompt: On-call is technically manageable but people hate it. Incidents are noisy, handoffs are poor, and nobody trusts the runbooks. What do you change first?

title: The data model argument
prompt: One engineer wants a normalized relational model. Another wants a document model because it matches the UI. Both are smart and both can make a good case. What decides it?

title: The deadline that requires quality debt
prompt: A launch date is fixed by a conference. The team can ship by cutting tests and observability. What do you say to the business and what do you change in the plan?

title: The status report that hides reality
prompt: Your manager wants a simple red-yellow-green status report. The project is yellow in five different ways. How do you communicate without turning complexity into a lie?

title: The refactor with no customer story
prompt: An engineer proposes a major refactor because the code is painful. There is no direct customer value and the team is behind on roadmap work. How do you decide?

title: The articulate candidate
prompt: A candidate is charismatic, uses all the right architecture vocabulary, and gives polished answers. Their examples are thin on concrete tradeoffs. What do you probe?

title: The product decision you think is wrong
prompt: Product wants to simplify a workflow by hiding advanced options. You think it will hurt expert users. How do you make the argument without turning it into a turf war?
